clue.text: Kind of bird that could transport one.

definitions.meaning: a marsh bird such as the water crake family
railway lines carry trains that move passengers

explanation.surface: A bird so big it could carry a passenger.
explanation.definitionFit: The crake family of wading birds shares its name with the track on which trains carry travellers.

clue.text: Not the gigantic type of sea comber.

definitions.text: Not the gigantic type of sea comber.

parts.words: Not the gigantic type of sea comber.
parts.note: a comber is usually a huge breaking wave, but here it is one who combs her hair while sitting in the sea

explanation.surface: Observing that this particular breaker on the beach is a small one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Comber' suggests a big rolling wave; the legendary sea-maiden is pictured combing her hair on a rock.
explanation.definitionFit: Folklore shows the half-fish sea-maiden combing her locks with a mirror in hand, so she is a sea comber.

clue.text: This' has' deep significance,

parts.note: deep here suggests profound meaning, but it is the depth of the open sea

explanation.surface: A remark that something is profoundly meaningful.
explanation.definitionFit: Anything belonging to the great seas relates to the deep, so it literally carries deep significance.

clue.text: Prize of a watch of sorts,

parts.note: ward means a watch or guard, as in the phrase watch and ward

explanation.surface: Someone receives a timepiece of some kind as a prize.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Watch' tempts as a timepiece; here it is guarding, the old sense kept in 'watch and ward'.
explanation.definitionFit: A prize is something given as a recognition of merit, a trophy or honour.

clue.text: Here's quite a proper howdy-do!

parts.note: a howdy-do usually means a fuss or commotion, but here it is a literal formal greeting

explanation.surface: An exclamation at a right old commotion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A proper howdy-do' is British slang for a fuss; read literally it is a correct 'how do you do' greeting.
explanation.definitionFit: Clasping and shaking palms is the conventional greeting that accompanies 'how do you do'.

clue.text: Presumably one good at a splice.

definitions.text: Presumably one good at a splice.

parts.words: Presumably one good at a splice.
parts.note: a splice joins rope ends, or joins a couple in marriage; someone skilled at it brings things together

explanation.surface: Describing a sailor who is skilled at joining ropes.
explanation.definitionFit: Splicing makes two pieces one, so whoever does it well is a maker of oneness.

clue.text: Interpret — no longer obvious, it seems.

parts.note: ex is a prefix meaning former

explanation.surface: Interpreting something once clear that now seems obscure.
explanation.definitionFit: To interpret something is to make its meaning clear to someone, to expound it.

clue.text: Catch a draught.

definitions.meaning: a catch of fish taken in one go
a draught of fishes is the quantity netted at one cast, as in the Gospel story

explanation.surface: Picking up a chill from a cold breeze.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Catch a draught' reads as catching a cold from a breeze; both halves mean a netful of fish.
explanation.definitionFit: A fisherman's take in one pull of the net is both a catch and, in Biblical language, a draught.

clue.text: Fearful rows they make!

parts.note: rows suggests loud quarrels, but also lines of big guns making a terrible din

explanation.surface: Complaining about people who make dreadful arguments.
explanation.definitionFit: A sustained barrage from lines of artillery makes a frightful noise.

clue.text: Elapsed maybe, tho' was agreeable

indicators.note: maybe says the letters of the word before it could be arranged another way

explanation.surface: Time has passed, though the person was content.
explanation.definitionFit: If something pleased someone, it was agreeable to them, gratifying them.

clue.text: It sets a plain standard.

parts.note: the idiom 'as plain as a ...' makes this long wooden shaft the benchmark of plainness

explanation.surface: Describing a rule that lays down a simple benchmark.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase 'plain as a pikestaff' uses the plain shaft of a spear as a byword for obviousness.

clue.text: Not a baby: who's left outside the front-door.

definitions.text: Not a baby: who's left outside the front-door.

parts.words: Not a baby: who's left outside the front-door.
parts.note: suggests a foundling left on a doorstep, but splits as the doorstep plus a youngster

explanation.surface: An infant abandoned outside a house.
explanation.walkthrough: The doorstep foundling image is the trap: the step plus a child gives the kin from a remarriage.
explanation.definitionFit: A spouse's offspring from an earlier marriage is a relation by remarriage, not one's own baby.

clue.text: Just fancy a monster like this!

definitions.text: Just fancy a monster like this!

parts.words: Just fancy a monster like this!
parts.note: fancy works as an exclamation, but also as a noun meaning an illusion; the word is also a fire-breathing beast

explanation.surface: An exclamation of amazement at seeing a monster.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek fire-breathing hybrid beast lends its name to any wild fantasy or illusion.

clue.text: I a pub hero? It could all be a plant!.

indicators.note: says all of the preceding words could be rearranged into something else

explanation.surface: Someone wonders if they are a pub hero and decides it could all be a ruse.

clue.text: Yet they aren't much use in walking the plank!

definitions.text: Yet they aren't much use in walking the plank!

parts.words: Yet they aren't much use in walking the plank!
parts.note: the steadiness a sailor gains on a rolling deck will not save a pirate's victim forced off the plank

explanation.surface: A grim joke about the pirate punishment of walking the plank.
explanation.definitionFit: A seasoned sailor's balance on a moving ship is called this, though it cannot help a doomed prisoner.

clue.text: Whence a sprinkle of wit?

parts.note: Attic salt is a phrase for refined wit, so the container for sprinkling salt is a source of wit

explanation.surface: Asking where a dash of humour comes from.
explanation.definitionFit: The table container you shake seasoning from; salt is an old figure for wit.

clue.text: Public, but limited as a form of transport,

definitions.text: limited as a form of transport,
definitions.meaning: a train stopping at every station serves only a limited area

explanation.surface: Public transport is described as limited.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'local' in Britain is one's nearby pub, the 'public house'.
explanation.definitionFit: A neighbourhood pub and a stopping train both serve only the nearby area.

clue.text: Swell, to very loud finale.

parts.note: ff is the musical marking fortissimo, very loud, placed at the end here

explanation.surface: Music swells to a very loud ending.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Swell' looks like a crescendo verb; it is a noun for a smart dandy.
explanation.definitionFit: A swell is old slang for a well-dressed upper-class gentleman.

clue.text: That sweet little-humbug!

definitions.meaning: a humbug is a mint sweet but also nonsense; the word is also an exclamation of 'nonsense'

explanation.surface: Calling a small mint candy a sweet.
explanation.walkthrough: A humbug is a British striped mint sweet, so the surface stays in the sweet shop; the second sense is nonsense.
explanation.definitionFit: The soft confection shares its name with the old exclamation dismissing something as nonsense.
